item.title: When in Doubt, Cry (or Bark) It Out
item.description:
Resilience

When in Doubt, Cry (or Bark) It Out

Personal Perspective: What can you do when you aren’t feeling resilient?

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Feeling weak doesn't mean you aren't resilient.
  • Giving your doubts an outlet can help you harness your inner strength.
  • Find relief in mindfulness, breath work, and emotional release.
Source: Tracy Strauss

A resilient person doesn’t always feel resilient. In fact, some days, resilient people feel utterly defeated. In the middle of a crisis, or a very bad month or week, doubt rushes in.

All my life, people have told me I’m “the strongest person” they know, that I’m “resilient.” Nothing stops me. They count on many fingers the scenarios and events and bad times I’ve overcome, moments they say they'd never survive. I'm not sure they give themselves enough credit for their triumphs. But that aside, yes, the fact is, when the going gets tough, I am dogged. And yet I, too, have times when I doubt that I can make it through, or even get out of bed.

What can you do when you aren’t feeling resilient, but need to find resilience?

  1. Find relief in simple things: I used to live in a very troubling housing situation in which there seemed to be no way out. Despite my efforts, I wasn’t able to secure a new place to live, for more than two years. Some days, I had a lot of trouble getting out of bed, but my dog had to go out, and so I got up and got dressed. On our walk, I looked for any simple pleasures or moments of meaning that I could find—a monarch butterfly fluttering around our busy, chaotic, loud neighborhood street; the wave and the smile of Sal, the friendly owner of the local gardening center across from our building, someone who always had a treat, a kind word, and an ear rub for my dog; the sound of birds chirping at the park; and the sunrise, the dark sky brightening into pink and purple hues while I stood in a field alone with my dog, savoring the peace and quiet before anyone else awakened.
  2. Mindful breathing: Studies have shown that breathwork can reduce the effects of stress. While slowing down our breath may be the last thing we think we can do when we’re stressed, breathing slowly and mindfully can actually be the antidote. Feeling trapped in my old neighborhood, I experienced panic attacks and developed severe acid reflux, symptoms I would later discover were tied to my nervous system’s dysregulation and my anxious breathing. As I began to practice controlled, mindful breathing before, during, and after eating (and, as much as I could, during extremely stressful moments), my symptoms improved. I was also able to stop a panic attack mid-event, by becoming mindful of my breath.
  3. Cry, scream, let it out: Releasing pent-up emotions can help us to feel more resilient by reducing stress hormones and shifting us out of the “fight or flight” response. Screaming can also help, or throwing things (safely). One day I felt I just couldn’t win: Everywhere I turned was another problem, another dead end, another fire I couldn’t put out. Then the actual fire alarms were set off in my building: It was “only” a test, the property management company said. Too bad for me that I was at home with my anxious dog, who was traumatized by the sound. On any other day, this situation might've just been a tiny nuisance, but in this instance, my cup of hot stress was already spilling over. We went outside to escape the noise just as a person on a scooter whizzed by, scaring my dog, who lunged and barked in reaction, physically releasing his own stress. The scooter rider looked and laughed as I was dragged halfway into the street. Many times before, I’d swallowed my anger and disgust at such insensitivity. This time, I screamed an expletive at the scooter rider. Perhaps it wasn't an admirable thing to do, but I felt a sense of release.
article continues after advertisement

I’m not advocating for cursing or screaming at people, but finding your voice, or any other productive way to step out of your despair, depression, anxiety, or your deep pain, can give you just the amount of space you need to get back to harnessing your strength.

Source: Tracy Strauss

I finally found a way to move, six weeks ago. And then my dog’s severe separation anxiety, which I thought I’d cured, returned with a vengeance. My ability to leave home solo quickly titrated to a trickle. With separation anxiety in dogs, a regression’s timeframe is indefinite. Once, Beau had a regression that lasted more than ten months. Other times, his regressions lasted a week or two. After over a year without any regression, and comfortable solo times for as much as four hours, I’d thought I’d put this problem behind me, but we are in the thick of it as I write this post and my world has shrunk. The more I can't leave, the harder it has been to think positively about the present and the future.

Today, when my attempt to leave brought on bark after bark, I felt overcome by debilitating doubt, uncertain I’d ever see a return to normal life, unless I were to give up my dog. That thought caused me to lose all composure. I wept for so long, I didn’t think I’d ever stop.

Somewhere in the middle of my emotional release, I heard a voice deep within: He’s done it before, and he’ll do it again. Be patient. You've got this.

Whenever you think you can't make it through a difficult time, give your doubt an outlet. Then go back to being dogged. You've got this.

item.title: Gender and Collecting
item.description:
Gender

Gender and Collecting

Do female collectors make different choices from male collectors, and if so, why?

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Neuroscience suggests that male and female brains are far more alike than different.
  • Collecting, then, cannot be explained as “women collect this” and “men collect that” in any rigid sense.
  • Gender may nudge collecting choices in subtle ways.

Neuroscience suggests that male and female brains are far more alike than different, with extensive overlap across individuals. Although researchers find some average sex differences in brain structure and function, these differences are generally small relative to the variation within each sex. That matters because collecting is shaped far more by personality, culture, opportunity, memory, and emotion than by any simple binary of “male brain” or “female brain.” Still, gendered experience may influence what people notice, value, organize, and preserve, potentially contributing to collection choices in subtle ways.

Popular accounts often overstate what the science shows. In brain research, group averages can be statistically real without being practically predictive for any one person, especially when distributions overlap so widely that some men may resemble women more than members of their own sex. Collecting, then, should not be explained as “women collect this” and “men collect that” in any rigid sense.

A visitor at Sotheby’s auction house in New York City admires a suit worn by Bob Dylan.
Source: Thomas M. Mueller Photography

Even so, there are pathways by which gendered experience could shape collecting preferences. Socialization affects what objects are presented as desirable, what hobbies are encouraged, how much room a person feels entitled to take up in a home, and which forms of knowledge are rewarded as “serious” or “frivolous.” A child who is praised for tidiness may become a collector of curated, orderly objects; another who is encouraged toward expertise may collect in ways that emphasize taxonomy, completeness, provenance, or investment value. In that sense, collecting is not simply a private preference but a behavioral archive of upbringing, identity, and social expectation.

The substance of collections may also reflect gendered pathways through life. Some people are drawn to objects that support caregiving, memory, beauty, or domestic continuity; others are drawn to technical, historical, or financial systems of value. Yet these tendencies are not owned by one sex or the other, and any observed differences are better understood as tendencies shaped by circumstances than as biological destiny. A woman who collects wine may be driven by sensory knowledge and social ritual; a man who collects fashionable clothing may be motivated by design history or nostalgia. The object itself tells us less than the meaning the collector assigns to it.

Research on gender and decision-making also cautions against overinterpreting differences in decision style. Such differences can be influenced by context, stress, confidence, and social norms rather than reflecting fixed traits. That is relevant to collecting because acquisition decisions are often decisions under uncertainty: Should I buy this now? Is this authentic? Will it matter later? Who else values it? In some settings, men and women may navigate these questions differently on average, but those differences are too mixed and too mutable to justify sweeping claims about taste or competence.

article continues after advertisement

Collecting also has a neuropsychological dimension that resists broad gender explanations. People collect to regulate affect, preserve identity, manage loss, build community, signal expertise, or create coherence in an unstable world, among other motives. Those reasons can be intensified by life stage, trauma, social isolation, wealth, and opportunity, none of which can be attributed to sex.

If gender contributes at all, it likely does so by filtering the route into collecting, not by dictating the outcome. Culture teaches people what to admire, what to save, what to display, and what to call expertise. Biology may contribute to broad constraints on temperament and reward sensitivity, but the actual collection—art, antiques, wine, dolls, tools, records, books, teapots, minerals, memorabilia—usually emerges from a highly personal mix of curiosity and chance. The result is not two kinds of collectors, but many kinds of humans.

That is the healthiest way to think about the topic: with respect for real differences, but far more for overlap, individuality, and context. Gender may nudge collecting choices at the margins; yet the larger story is that people collect because objects help them remember, organize, and express who they are.

item.title: From Bufo Toad Venom to Big Pharma
item.description:
Addiction

From Bufo Toad Venom to Big Pharma

How a desert psychedelic molecule may become a modern antidepressant.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Research on synthetic 5-MeO-DMT has advanced from early observational studies to positive clinical trials.
  • Scientists have moved from natural toad secretions to standardized 5-MeO-DMT pharmaceutical formulations.
  • Major questions remain regarding durability, optimal dosing, placebo effects, and long-term safety.

Earlier this year, I wrote about one of psychiatry's most unusual drug-development stories: a psychedelic compound first identified in the defensive secretions of the Sonoran Desert toad that has now entered the realm of randomized clinical trials for severe depression. The field has advanced dramatically beyond the early period when the compound was known primarily through recreational use and colorful names such as Bufo, Sapito, "the toad," and even "the Joe Rogan psychedelic." Today's scientific story, however, has surprisingly little to do with the toad itself.

Many medicines began with unexpected observations in nature. Aspirin originated from willow bark. Penicillin emerged from mold. Psilocybin was isolated from naturally occurring mushrooms; GLP-1 receptor agonists owe part of their development to studies of Gila monster saliva. In each case, scientists did not simply use the natural source—they identified the active molecule, developed standardized pharmaceutical formulations, and rigorously tested them. The story of 5-MeO-DMT appears to be following that same path.

The first randomized, placebo-controlled Phase 2b trial of inhaled synthetic 5-MeO-DMT has now reported robust antidepressant effects in patients with treatment-resistant depression, moving the field well beyond the small open-label studies that initially generated excitement. Cubala and colleagues’ study is now the landmark clinical study in the field. Participants experienced large reductions in depression severity, remission rates approaching 60 percent after a single treatment day, and no serious adverse events during the blinded phase. Psychiatric researchers have searched for faster and more effective antidepressants for decades. These findings represent an important milestone.

From Desert Toad to Modern Antidepressant
Source: Mark Gold, MD, used with permission

If ongoing studies continue to confirm clinical benefit, psychiatry may be looking at a carefully supervised intervention measured in minutes rather than months.

The momentum became even more apparent when Eli Lilly disclosed plans to acquire AtaiBeckley for up to $3.8 billion, largely to obtain BPL-003, an intranasal formulation of synthetic 5-MeO-DMT. Of course, a multibillion-dollar acquisition does not guarantee FDA approval. But when one of the world's largest neuroscience companies believes the science has matured enough to justify a major investment, attention is paid. The attraction is not simply to acquire another psychedelic. The possibility is far more ambitious: a medicine that can be administered in less than 30 minutes yet produce antidepressant benefits lasting weeks—or perhaps months—after a single supervised treatment.

article continues after advertisement

More broadly, the acquisition indicates a changing landscape in psychiatry. Psychedelic medicines have moved outside academic laboratories and small biotechnology companies into mainstream pharmaceutical development. Just as Janssen's development of esketamine helped establish rapid-acting antidepressants, Lilly's investment may accelerate the next generation of neuroplasticity-based therapies.

A Different Therapeutic Model

Perhaps the most intriguing aspect of 5-MeO-DMT is not that it appears to act rapidly—it’s how brief the treatment itself may be.

Traditional antidepressants typically require daily administration for weeks before patients experience meaningful improvement. Ketamine can produce relief within hours but generally requires repeated infusions or intranasal treatments, with each visit involving prolonged monitoring. By contrast, inhaled synthetic 5-MeO-DMT produces an intense but remarkably brief psychedelic experience, usually lasting only 15 to 30 minutes. If larger studies verify that combination of rapid-onset, short treatment duration, and durable benefit, 5-MeO-DMT could become one of the most practical psychedelic-assisted therapies currently under development.

Despite encouraging findings, many important questions remain. One challenge is that psychedelic trials are inherently difficult to blind. Most participants can recognize whether they received an active psychedelic, making expectancy effects difficult to separate from true pharmacologic benefit. Investigators are refining study designs to minimize this limitation.

Durability is also still uncertain. How long will improvement last after a single treatment? Which patients will require repeat dosing? Can additional treatments safely maintain remission?

These questions will become increasingly important as larger Phase 3 trials move forward.

Safety also deserves continued attention. The experience with synthetic 5-MeO-DMT has been reassuring when treatment occurs under carefully controlled medical conditions. In these studies, patients are carefully screened before treatment. People with a personal or family history of bipolar disorder or schizophrenia are generally not enrolled. Participants receive a standardized pharmaceutical formulation and are monitored by experienced clinical teams before, during, and after treatment.

article continues after advertisement

That is very different from recreational use or the use of natural toad secretions.

Outside of research or specialized treatment settings, there is no careful screening, no standardized dose, and no medical supervision. People may use unknown or impure preparations, combine them with other drugs or alcohol, or have underlying psychiatric or medical conditions that increase the risk of serious adverse effects, including prolonged psychological distress or psychosis in susceptible individuals.

As with electroconvulsive therapy, ketamine, transcranial magnetic stimulation, and every major advance in psychiatry before them, the full safety profile of synthetic 5-MeO-DMT will become clear only through larger clinical trials, longer follow-up, and, if approved, careful post-marketing surveillance.

A New Way of Thinking About Depression

Psychiatry has customarily relied on medications taken every day to gradually modify brain chemistry. But psychedelic-assisted therapies suggest a different possibility: brief interventions capable of producing rapid and potentially lasting changes in brain circuits involved in mood, cognition, and affective processing. Exactly how these benefits occur remains an active area of investigation. They may reflect enhanced neuroplasticity, profound psychological experiences, or—as is often true in medicine—a blend of biological and psychological systems working together.

From my perspective, one of the most interesting possibilities is that psychedelics may help shift the brain from a maladaptive depressive state toward a healthier adaptive state. Whether this represents true circuit remodeling, psychological transformation, or both remains an important question for future research.

One useful way to appreciate the potential of 5-MeO-DMT is to compare it with other rapidly acting investigational antidepressants. Ketamine can relieve depressive symptoms within hours but generally requires repeated treatment sessions lasting one to two hours, including monitoring. Psilocybin-assisted therapy, the most studied psychedelic treatment for treatment-resistant depression, has demonstrated encouraging and durable antidepressant effects after one or two sessions. But psilocybin treatment usually requires six or more hours of clinical supervision. LSD is also under investigation for depression and anxiety, but its effects often extend 8 to 12 hours, making treatment considerably more demanding for both patients and treatment centers.

article continues after advertisement

By comparison, inhaled synthetic 5-MeO-DMT typically produces an intense psychedelic experience lasting only 15 to 30 minutes, yet early clinical trials suggest antidepressant benefits that may persist well beyond the acute drug experience. Whether its ultimate efficacy matches or exceeds these other psychedelics or treatments with fewer side effects remains unknown.

Medicine advances by replacing intriguing observations with rigorous evidence. Synthetic 5-MeO-DMT has now crossed that threshold. Whether it ultimately becomes an approved antidepressant is still uncertain, but randomized clinical trials—not anecdotes—are now driving the conversation.

Whether BPL-003 ultimately succeeds will depend on Phase 3 trials, long-term safety, and regulatory review. But one thing has already changed. The conversation has shifted from folklore to pharmacology, from anecdote to randomized clinical trials, and from curiosity to one of the most closely watched programs in modern neuropsychopharmacology. The story may have begun with a desert toad. Its future will be decided by science.

item.title: Be Ready for Your Visit to the Art Fair
item.description:
Environment

Be Ready for Your Visit to the Art Fair

Art can make your life significantly better.

Posted July 28, 2026

It’s art fair season! As you’re strolling through an art festival on a lovely summer day, what pieces should you bring home? Which ones will have the most positive effects on your life?

For our purposes today, let’s describe art as paintings, photographs, sculptures, etc., that we choose to surround ourselves with because we like to look at them—and our “art” can be full-size or reduced to fit on a postcard, original, or a reproduction. For our current discussion, we’ll ignore audio art (like music), kinesthetic art (such as dance), literature, and drama, etc. We’ll be focusing on the sorts of stuff you might encounter on display in the Louvre or the Metropolitan Museum of Art or your local art gallery.

The reason that most of us add art to our world is that doing so gives us a big psychological push toward wellbeing, at least when we get to select it (Chatterjee, 2013).

Choosing art is a way we can exercise some control over our lives and just doing that gives us a more positive mindset to meet the world and helps our brains work more effectively, regularly improving our cognitive performance (Dutton, 2009).

Via art, we can also signal to anyone who visits our home or wanders by our workspace what we value about ourselves, which might be that we’re good at our jobs, or a member of a particular group, or something else entirely. When we send these signals, we remind ourselves who we really are and give others clues not only about what drives us forward but also how to interact with us—and not just what to talk about. For example, if the art seen indicates that we live our lives in a relatively formal way, people know to stand a little farther from us when we talk; people who are more formal tend to prefer slightly larger personal space zones.

The Unique Appeal of Nature in Art

Art can also help us decompress and revitalize, particularly if it shows nature scenes.

  • The vacation photographs that seem to get the most “oohs” and “aahs” are always shots of nature. Whether they’re landscape or portrait, tropical or deciduous, with or without wildlife doesn’t seem to matter much. We like looking at images of nature, whether we’ve photographed a scene ourselves or not (Herzog, Maguire, and Nebel, 2003).
  • Our fondness for nature scenes makes sense, particularly if the sites shown look like they’re complete with the resources that would have been handy, survival-wise, for our species when it was young (Dutton, 2009). It seems that all the sensory processing circuits in our brains have developed to find it desirable to encounter the sorts of conditions that would have signaled to us that food was likely nearby and escape from predators that found us tasty would be possible (Dutton, 2009). According to Dutton (2009), these responses are so fundamental that just looking at the sorts of spaces where we would have thrived eons ago gives us a psychological boost, improving our mood and cognitive performance.
  • When we see nature scenes, either in photographs or in paintings, our stress levels fall, our mental performance improves, and we are mentally refreshed (Herzog, Maguire, and Nebel, 2003).
  • The sorts of nature scenes that are most useful for elevating our mental state are images that seem ready for us to step into (Dutton, 2009). Our brains do realize we won’t be able to merge into an image, even though that seems to happen all the time in movies (For example, have you seen the scene when Mary Poppins steps into the chalk drawing?), but we like to think we could. A relatively clear foreground, without a blocking hedge or fence, for example, is something we feel we can step into.
  • The “best” nature images feature clumps of trees that look ready for climbing spread across a meadow (Dutton, 2009). It’s fine if there’s some sign of human life, say a cottage in the distance or a gently curving road, but the weather should be stellar and the terrain in relatively good shape (not recently decimated by a wildfire, for example). Bonus mental welfare points accrue if there is a gently burbling brook or peaceful lake in view. Signs of nearby predators—say lions, tigers, or bears—are undesirable, as are jungle-like plant growth that would make it difficult for humans to see trouble approaching. Research also shows that seeing close-up images of flowers, ones where the blooms fill the frame, but stems aren’t obvious, can speed our return to normal after we’ve been stressed.
  • Images of nature can help us live our best lives and avoid being debilitated by everyday stressors (Herzog, Maguire, and Nebel, 2003). Nature images will work for you, even if you don’t have much time (vacation or otherwise) to work on them. Fancy printing and frames aren’t required for positive returns on effort invested.
  • We’re more positive about the art we create ourselves than we are about art made by others, so try, at least, to be objective about which of your own pieces you choose to display.

Consciously use art to brighten your life and to achieve your personal and professional objectives.
